_about: The learn-to-swim program's ladder (the plan: real/plan/swim_plan.md, whose last section is printed from this file; his notes as written: real/plan/learn_to_swim_notes.md). Four stages, twenty milestones, each titled in his tracker's own words (stage 2 puts 'Recover from floating to standing' before 'Float independently': knowing how to stand up is what makes floating alone safe). skill = the session block it is worked in (config.json -> swim.skills). judged = how it is called done. needs = the milestones that come first: one is 'ready' when its needs are done, and the next pool session is built from what is ready, so the plan follows what he has done, never the calendar. work = the drills that lead to it, in order, each to be easy before the next. stuck = what to do when it stalls. knee = what the left knee asks. target = his own planning estimate for the stage: a target, never a deadline. done = null until it happens, then {date, evidence, witness}. cleared = the PT's word on the pool ({date, evidence}; the master plan lists swimming 'as cleared'): until it is recorded, what is logged in the pool is kept and pays nothing. session = the frame of a visit: the blocks in order, each with its usual minutes and what it shrinks to (`keep`) once its milestones are all done. The drills and the judging are general adult learn-to-swim practice, proposed 11/27: an instructor's word, or the PT's on the knee, outranks any line here. Written by `darrow.py swim pass|clear|cleared` (done, cleared); the rest is edited when the plan changes.

session.length: 45 to 60 minutes, once a week, with a buddy who can swim and a lifeguard on duty

blocks.title: Warm-up
blocks.text: In by the steps or the ladder. Water walking forward, backward and sideways in chest-deep water, shoulders under; three slow breaths out with your mouth at the surface.

blocks.title: Underwater breathing
blocks.keep: 5 slow bobs: under, bubbles out through the nose, up, one breath in.

blocks.title: Floating, recovery and rolling
blocks.keep: One back float and one front float, 20 seconds each, standing up out of each; three rolls front to back.

blocks.title: Treading water
blocks.keep: One minute afloat, any calm way you like.

blocks.title: Swimming
blocks.keep: One easy length by any stroke, rolling to your back for a breath whenever you want one.

blocks.title: Deep water
blocks.keep: The deep end is yours: swim there because you want to.

blocks.title: Cool-down
blocks.text: An easy back float or water walking. Say one thing that felt better than last week. Out by the steps.

milestones.title: Submerge my head without pinching my nose
milestones.judged: head fully under in standing-depth water with both hands off the nose, three times in one visit
work: Bubbles at the surface: chin in the water, hum through your nose so the water in front of your face ripples. 5 slow breaths out. From here on your hands stay on the wall or on your thighs, never near your face.
Nose in: start the hum, lower until the water covers your nose, come up. 5 times. The hum is what keeps the water out, so it starts before you go under and stops after you are up.
Eyes in, goggles on: hum, lower until the goggles are under, look at your own hands for a slow count of 3, come up. 5 times.
All the way: hum, sink until the top of your head is wet, count 3, stand. Three in a row with your hands on your thighs is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: Water up the nose means the breath out stopped or the chin tipped back: tuck the chin a little, hum louder, and come up before the air runs out, never after. A nose clip for a visit or two is a fair bridge for every other block; take it off for this one.

milestones.title: Exhale gently through my nose underwater
milestones.judged: a slow, steady stream of bubbles through the nose for about five seconds, three times in one visit (no forceful humming)
work: The slow leak: face in, let the air out through the nose as thin as you can make it. Count how many seconds the stream lasts. 5 tries; aim for 5 seconds.
One long 'mmmm' under water on one breath. If the bubbles come out in a burst, you pushed: start again, quieter.
Bobs: under with bubbles, up for one easy breath in through the mouth, straight back under. 5 in a row, then 10. This rhythm is the one that will look after you in deep water.
milestones.stuck: Running out of air in two seconds means you are blowing, not leaking. Add one second to the stream each visit. The shower is where this gets easy: the same hum with the spray on your face.

milestones.title: Resurface calmly
milestones.judged: up from a full submersion with no gasp, no grab for the wall and no rush to wipe the face, three times in one visit
work: Come up slowly: rise until your mouth is clear, let the water run off, and only then breathe in. Hands stay down: no wiping, no reaching.
Finish the breath out as your mouth clears the surface, so that the first thing you do in the air is breathe in.
Say one calm word out loud after each one before you do anything else. Three in a row is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: Coming up with a gasp means you stayed down too long: cut the time under to a count of 2 and build back up. Coming up calm matters more than staying down long.

milestones.title: Feel comfortable with my ears underwater
milestones.judged: ears under for about 30 seconds while breathing normally (a supported back float counts), and his own word that it felt fine
work: Standing, holding the wall: lean one ear into the water, then the other, then tip your head back until both are under. Listen to how quiet it is. 5 slow breaths.
The cradle: your buddy stands behind you with a hand under the back of your head. Lean back until your ears are under, eyes on the ceiling, feet still on the bottom. 3 times, 10 seconds each.
The same with the hand between your shoulder blades and your feet off the bottom. Work up to 30 seconds of ordinary breathing.
milestones.stuck: If the feeling of water in your ears is the whole problem, wear earplugs and move on. A tight neck means you are holding your head up: let the water take its weight.

milestones.title: Float on my back with assistance
milestones.judged: a back float held about 15 seconds with a hand under the shoulders, ears in the water
work: From the cradle (ears in, a hand under your head), have your buddy slide the hand down to between your shoulder blades. Arms out wide, palms up, chin a little up.
Breathe low and slow. A full breath lifts you; let half of it out, feel yourself settle, fill again. 15 seconds with the hand there is the milestone.
Then the hand becomes two fingers, then hovers under you without touching. Ask not to be told when it lets go.
milestones.stuck: Legs that drop are normal for lean, muscular legs: let them hang, or add a small slow kick from the hips. A float with the legs low and the face dry is a float. With no buddy that day, a noodle under your knees or a kickboard hugged to your chest stands in.

milestones.title: Recover from floating to standing
milestones.judged: from a back float and from a front float, feet back under him and standing with no help, three times each
work: From the back: tuck your knees toward your chest, drop your chin, and scoop both hands forward as if pulling a chair under you. Your feet swing down; stand. 5 with your buddy's hand there, then 5 without.
From the front (holding the wall or your buddy's hands, face in, legs floating): pull your knees under you, press down with both hands, lift your head last. Stand. 5 times.
Then let go: a front float from standing (arms forward, face in, count 3) and stand up out of it by yourself. Three each way is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: Lifting the head first is what makes the feet miss the floor: knees in first, head last. Do it in water no deeper than your ribs until it is automatic. This is the skill that makes every float safe, so it comes before floating alone.
milestones.knee: Both feet go down together and softly.

milestones.title: Float independently
milestones.judged: a back float held about 15 seconds with no one touching him; a small kick or scull to keep the legs up counts (lean legs sink)
work: Push-off float: crouch with your shoulders under and your back to the open water, lean back until your ears are in, and let your feet come up by themselves. Count 5, stand. Add 2 seconds a try.
Find your balance: arms stretched back past your head moves weight that way and lifts the legs; arms at your sides drops them. Try both, keep what works.
The working float: a slow flutter kick from the hips and small sculling circles with your hands by your sides, only enough to keep your legs near the surface. 15 seconds untouched is the milestone.
The front float too: face in, arms forward, legs long, 5 to 10 seconds, stand.
milestones.stuck: Stiff is what sinks. Before each try, one long breath out through the nose with your face in, shoulders dropped. If the fear is of not being held, have your buddy stand an arm's length away with hands in the water, not on you.
milestones.knee: Kick from the hips with long legs. No frog kick.

milestones.title: Roll from front to back
milestones.judged: from a front float or glide, roll onto the back and breathe without touching the bottom, three times, unassisted
work: On the wall: hold the gutter with one hand, float face down, and turn your whole body like a log toward the open side until you are looking at the ceiling. Keep hold. 5 each way.

With hands: your buddy holds your hips lightly while you front float with bubbles for a count of 3, then roll: one shoulder drops, the head turns with the body, the chin comes up last. Two breaths on your back. 5 times.
Alone: a front glide off the wall, bubbles for 3, roll, breathe, float, stand. Three in a row without touching is the milestone.
Back to front as well, so you can go under, look where you are going, and come back up for air.
milestones.stuck: Lifting your head to breathe before the roll finishes sinks you: the head stays in line and the eyes follow the shoulder. Slow is fine, with bubbles all the way round.

milestones.title: Swim 10 yards continuously
milestones.judged: 10 yards by any stroke without touching the bottom or the wall, in standing-depth water
work: Glides first: push off the wall on your front, arms long, face in, bubbles, and see how far one push carries you. Stand. Then the same on your back. 4 each.
Add the kick: the same glides with a small quick flutter kick from the hips, legs long, toes pointed, knees soft. On the back first, where you can breathe, then the front.

The back is the easy road. On your back, kicking, add a slow double-arm pull: hands slide up your sides to your armpits, reach out, sweep down to your thighs, glide. Most adults make 10 yards this way within a few visits.
On the front: glide, kick, and reach with big slow pulls. When you want air, roll to your back, take two breaths, and roll back or stay there. That counts.
Measure it: ask the lifeguard where 10 yards is (usually a little past the first flags).
milestones.stuck: Leave the front crawl's side breathing for later: it is the hardest thing in swimming and this milestone does not need it. Tiring in 5 yards means kicking from the knees or holding your breath: longer legs, steady bubbles.
milestones.knee: Flutter kick only, in a straight line from the hip. No frog or whip kick and no fins until the PT says so. Push off the wall gently, with both feet.

milestones.title: Swim 25 yards continuously
milestones.judged: one 25-yard length by any stroke without touching the bottom or the wall
work: Build by landmarks: 10 yards, then to the far flags, then the wall. One longer try a visit, after two or three easy ones.

Swim, float, swim: on your front for as long as it is comfortable, roll to your back and rest there with a gentle kick, roll back. A length done this way counts, and it is the pattern that gets a tired swimmer home.
Slow down: three kicks to each arm pull, and a glide. A length that takes a minute is a better length than one that takes 30 seconds and leaves you gasping.
Swim in the lane beside the wall, in water you can stand in the whole way if the pool has it.
milestones.stuck: A stall around 15 yards is breath, not strength: make the first half deliberately lazy. If lifting your head sinks your legs, do the whole length on your back.
milestones.knee: Flutter kick only until the PT clears another; easy push-offs.

milestones.title: Tread water for 30 seconds
milestones.judged: head above the surface for 30 seconds with nothing touching the bottom or the wall (in standing depth with the feet up, or deep and supervised)
work: Hands first, standing with your shoulders under: sculling. Palms down, sweep both hands out and in as if smoothing sand, thumbs tilted down on the way out and up on the way in. You should feel the water push up on your palms. 3 rounds of 20 seconds.
Legs second, holding the wall or a noodle: a slow bicycle, or a small flutter kick straight below you, body upright.
Together, feet off the floor: in chest-deep water, scull and kick with your knees drawn up so your feet clear the bottom. 5 seconds, stand. Then 10, 15, 20, 30.
Slow and wide beats fast and small: head tipped back a little, mouth just clear, lungs full.
milestones.stuck: Sinking to the eyebrows means you are trying to hold too much of yourself out of the water: only your face needs to be dry. If the legs will not carry it yet, tread with a noodle under your arms and take it away a visit later.
milestones.knee: The kick is the knee's question. Slow bicycle or flutter only, in a straight line. The frog kick and the eggbeater twist the knee: they wait for the PT's word.

milestones.title: Float or tread water for 1 minute
milestones.judged: one minute afloat by floating, treading or both, nothing touching
work: Mix it: 20 seconds treading, roll onto your back and float for 20, come back up and tread for 20. Changing over is the skill.
Add 10 seconds a visit to whichever part is easier, and hold the other where it is.
Do it once fresh and once near the end of the session, when you are a little tired.
milestones.stuck: If the treading runs out first, let the back float carry most of the minute. This one is about staying up by any calm means.

milestones.title: Float or tread water for 2 minutes
milestones.judged: two minutes afloat by floating, treading or both, nothing touching
work: Two minutes is pacing. Start slower than you think you need to and breathe in a pattern: in for 2, out for 4.
Give yourself jobs while you are up there: turn a full circle, find the nearest exit, hold one hand out of the water for 5 seconds, say the alphabet.
Once it is easy in standing depth, do it within arm's reach of the wall where the water is over your head, supervised.
milestones.stuck: A stall around 90 seconds is usually tight shoulders: drop them, widen the scull, and lean back onto the water a little.

milestones.title: Pass a supervised water competency assessment
milestones.judged: the Red Cross sequence in one go, supervised: into water over his head and back to the surface, float or tread for one minute, turn a full circle and find the exit, swim 25 yards to it, and get out without the ladder
work: Rehearse the five parts one at a time in the deep end, beside the wall: step in where it is over your head and come back up; float or tread for a minute; turn one full circle and point at your exit; swim 25 yards to it; get out without the ladder.
Getting out without the ladder: both hands flat on the deck, bob down once and use the rise to press up to straight arms, turn and sit. It is an arm exercise.

Chain them two at a time (the entry and the minute; the minute, the circle and the swim), then all five. Ask a lifeguard or an instructor to watch the whole sequence: many pools run it as their swim test.
milestones.stuck: The part that fails is nearly always the minute afloat straight after the entry, because the entry spends your calm. Take three slow breaths on your back before you start counting.
milestones.knee: The step in is a feet-first entry into deep water, so there is no landing. The climb out can put a knee on the deck: kneeling on the left is allowed to comfort and not pushed (PT 16), so lead with the right, or use the ladder until it is comfortable and finish that part later.

milestones.title: Swim in deep water with confidence
milestones.judged: two visits in a row swimming in water over his head, supervised, each of which he rates calm (4 or 5 of 5)
work: Rung 1, the wall: hand over hand along the gutter from the shallow end to the deep end and back, shoulders under. Stop over the deep water and look down through your goggles. Twice.
Rung 2, under and up: holding the gutter with both hands in the deep end, 5 bobs: arms straight, under with bubbles, pull up, breathe.
Rung 3, letting go: one hand off, then both, for a count of 1, then 2, then 5, sculling and kicking. The wall stays within reach.
Rung 4, floating it: back to the wall, lean back into a float with your head toward the middle of the lane, count 10, roll, and take two strokes back to the wall.
Rung 5, leaving and coming back (once you can swim 10 yards): push gently off the wall, glide a body length out, turn round, swim back. Then two lengths out.
Rung 6, along the wall (once you can stay afloat a minute): swim the deep half of a length in the lane beside the wall, your buddy walking the deck beside you.
Rung 7, across the line: swim from where you can stand to where you cannot, and on to the far wall. Then start from the deep end. Two visits in a row of this, each rated calm, is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: Stay on a rung for as many visits as it takes to be bored there: boredom is the signal to move up. If a rung sends your heart racing, drop back one, do that one well once, and end the block there. This block is never done without a lifeguard on duty and someone on the deck who knows what you are working on.

milestones.title: Perform a supervised feet-first deep-water entry
milestones.judged: a step or a jump in, feet first, where the water is over his head, supervised
work: Slide in: sit on the edge at the deep end, hands on the deck beside you, turn and lower yourself in holding the wall. Then the same, letting go as you go under and coming back up to the wall.
From sitting: lean forward and push off with your hands so you drop in feet first a foot from the wall, bubbles through the nose all the way down and up. Turn, take the wall.

The step: stand at the edge with your toes over it, look at the far wall and not down, take one big step out and bring your feet together. Press your arms down through the water as you go under to stop the drop. Up, breathe, three breaths on your back, swim to the wall. One supervised step or jump is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: If the drop is the fear, stay with the seated entry until it is dull. If the fear is of not coming up, do 5 deep-end bobs on the wall first: the water pushes you up every single time.
milestones.knee: Deep water only, so the feet touch nothing. Never jump or step into water you can stand in: that is a landing on a hard floor, and the leg's landings are still being built. Ask the PT before the first jump from the deck; until then the slide in is the entry.

milestones.title: Jump into deep water without holding my nose
milestones.judged: a jump into deep water with both hands away from the face
work: Start the hum before you leave the deck. The breath out through the nose begins in the air and does not stop until your face is back in the air.
Give your hands a job: arms out to the sides, or each hand holding the opposite elbow across your chest.
Steps in first, then a small two-foot jump out from the edge. Three good ones a visit is plenty.
milestones.stuck: Water up the nose on the way in means the hum stopped or the chin lifted: chin level, eyes on the far wall, a louder hum. A nose clip is no failure, but this milestone is done without one.
milestones.knee: A jump is a push-off from the deck: the PT's word first.

milestones.title: Resurface and swim to the wall calmly
milestones.judged: after a jump: up, a breath, and an unhurried swim to the wall, three times in one visit
work: Say the routine before you go: up, breathe, look, swim. Come up, take one full breath (on your back if you like), find the wall with your eyes, and swim to it at your slow-length pace.
Go in further out each time: a foot from the wall, then a body length, then from the corner so that the swim back is 5 or 10 yards.
Three in one visit, each unhurried, is the milestone.
milestones.stuck: If you race for the wall, add a rule: 5 seconds of treading or back floating after every entry before you are allowed to swim.

milestones.title: Perform a safe headfirst dive with an instructor
milestones.judged: a headfirst entry taught and watched by an instructor, in a designated diving area
work: This one is taught, so book the lesson. It happens only in a marked diving area (the Red Cross asks for at least 9 feet of water for a dive from the deck) and nowhere else: never the shallow end, a lake, a river or a hotel pool.

The usual ladder, each rung with the instructor: a sitting dive from the edge (arms locked over your ears, hands together, roll forward); a kneeling dive; a compact dive from a crouch; a standing dive.
Your arms stay locked over your head until you have surfaced: the hands meet the water, not the head, and they steer you up.
milestones.stuck: A belly flop means the head came up: chin to chest, eyes on your knees as you roll in. Stay with the sitting dive until it is clean. Nobody needs the standing dive on a schedule.
milestones.knee: The kneeling dive puts a knee on the deck: use a mat and kneel on the right, or skip that rung with the instructor's agreement. A standing dive's push-off is a small jump: ask the PT, though by then it should be long cleared.

milestones.title: Enjoy deep-water swimming
milestones.judged: his own word, after a visit in deep water he stayed in because he wanted to
work: One visit with no drills: get in at the deep end, float, swim where you like, get out when you want.
Notice what you choose to do when nothing is assigned. That is what the pool is for from now on.
milestones.stuck: If it still feels like a test, it is not this milestone's day yet. Nothing about it can be forced.
